Nestlings of the Western screech owl typically emerge from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] over a period of 26 days [ab = 26 days], a developmental duration that aligns with patterns observed in other small strigiforms. At the moment of hatching, these altricial neonates exhibit a wet weight at birth of approximately 14.01 grams [Wwb = approximately 14.01 grams], a modest mass reflecting the substantial energetic investment yet to be made by provisioning adults. This initial body mass, however, belies the rapid growth trajectory that characterizes the nestling phase, during which chicks transition from complete dependence on yolk reserves to receiving frequent deliveries of prey items. The relatively precise incubation period, recorded under controlled captive conditions, offers a baseline for understanding how thermal regimes during embryonic development may influence early-life phenotypes in wild populations occupying diverse climatic gradients across the species' range from coastal British Columbia to interior Mexico. Parental care begins almost immediately upon hatching, with both adults participating in brooding and food delivery to the developing chicks.

Females of this species achieve an ultimate wet weight of 194 grams [Wwi = 194 grams] at adulthood, while males are markedly smaller, reaching a maximum recorded adult body mass of 167 grams [Wwi = 167 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with females roughly 16 percent heavier than males, is typical among owls and is often attributed to the energetic demands of egg production and incubation, as well as the need for females to maintain body condition during the extended period of brooding. The initial weight of newly hatched chicks has been documented at 17.3 grams [Ww0 = 17.3 grams], representing a substantial proportional increase relative to the wet weight at birth, likely reflecting water absorption and the early onset of feeding. Juvenile birds undergo a period of rapid mass gain in the first weeks post-hatching, with growth rates influenced by prey availability and the frequency of parental provisioning visits. Comparisons with congeneric species such as Megascops asio suggest that these body mass values are near the upper end of the size spectrum for small screech owls inhabiting temperate forests.

Under the active metabolic conditions typical of this species, recorded at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], fledging occurs at 28 days after hatching [tx = 28 days after hatching], marking the achievement of sustained flight capability. This developmental milestone initiates the post-fledging period, during which young birds remain in proximity to the natal territory and continue to receive food from their parents for several additional weeks while refining their hunting skills. The relatively brief nestling period, compared to larger owl species, reflects the trade-off between predation risk in the nest and the advantages of early departure into a structurally complex environment where crypticity can be maintained. Following fledging, juveniles undergo a gradual transition to nutritional independence, with parental provisioning typically declining as the young birds become more proficient at capturing arthropods and small vertebrates. The timing of this transition is critical, as it must be synchronized with seasonal peaks in prey abundance to ensure adequate energy intake during the vulnerable post-fledging phase.

Gonadal maturation, assessed under captive conditions at a stable body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], is attained at 84 days after hatching [tp = 84 days after hatching], a relatively accelerated pace of sexual development among small owls that may facilitate early territory establishment. The first successful breeding event typically occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], indicating that while physiological puberty is achieved within the first three months, actual reproductive activity is deferred until the following breeding season, a pattern that allows young birds to invest fully in somatic growth and the acquisition of a high-quality nesting territory at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This temporal gap between sexual maturation and first reproduction is ecologically significant, as it reflects the competitive constraints faced by first-year birds in securing suitable nest cavities and sufficient foraging grounds. Field studies have confirmed that yearling individuals rarely breed successfully unless high-quality territories are available, suggesting that age at first reproduction is modulated by population density and habitat saturation rather than physiological limitation alone.

The maximum lifespan recorded for Megascops kennicottii in the wild, observed under natural thermal conditions approximating 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], reaches approximately 6,935 days [am = approximately 6,935 days], which corresponds to nearly 19 years, a value that places this species among the longer-lived small owls and likely reflects the low extrinsic mortality associated with its predatory lifestyle and defended nest cavities, though most individuals do not survive beyond the first few years due to predation and environmental stochasticity. Reproductive output is constrained by a modest clutch size of 3 to 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 to 4 eggs per clutch] combined with a single clutch produced each year [F_R_i = single clutch produced each year], a conservative life-history strategy typical of strigiforms that balances the high energetic costs of rearing altricial young against the relatively low annual mortality of adults. This annual reproductive rate, while low compared to passerines of similar body mass, is compensated by the species' extended reproductive lifespan, allowing multiple breeding attempts over the course of a decade or more. Long-term monitoring of marked individuals has provided valuable demographic data, revealing that survival rates decline noticeably after eight years of age, with senescence ultimately limiting the contribution of older breeders to population recruitment.
